## Why we tested this

<div class="callout callout-green">

We are **not proposing to redesign the entire trail system from a desk**.

We used one small area of Mercer County Park as a case study to understand what the existing data can support, where it becomes ambiguous, and what a better field-collection workflow could look like.

</div>

The goal is to come to Parks with something concrete to react to — not to tell Parks what its trails should be called or how they should be managed.

---

## What we started with

<div class="two-col">

<div class="card">

### Existing Parks data

- Trail centerlines already exist
- Individual features often represent pieces of a larger route
- Many features carry broad names such as **Red Trail**
- Some routes continue for long distances through multiple intersections
- Connectors, shared corridors, and unnamed pieces are mixed into the same underlying network

</div>

<div class="card">

### What GIS is trying to build

- A clear public-facing trail map
- Routes that make sense to someone standing in the park
- Better support for maintenance, closures, inspections, and future field work
- A structure that lets Parks keep detailed internal data **without exposing internal GIS complexity to the public**

</div>

</div>

---

## The case study

<div class="callout">

In one small area, three existing features were all part of the **Red Trail**. Two of those features continued well beyond the area, but portions of all three visually formed a smaller loop.

</div>

From a visitor perspective, that raised a simple question:

<div class="big-question">

Does one very long trail name need to be the only way this area is presented to the public?

</div>

<span class="small-note">“Proposed Loop A” is only a temporary GIS concept name used to test the idea.</span>

---

## What we actually did

<div class="step">
<div class="step-num">1</div>
<div>
<strong>Kept the existing geometry as our starting point.</strong><br>
We did not redraw the trail from scratch.
</div>
</div>

<div class="step">
<div class="step-num">2</div>
<div>
<strong>Identified where the short trail connected into the longer Red Trail.</strong><br>
Those connection locations became conceptual junction points.
</div>
</div>

<div class="step">
<div class="step-num">3</div>
<div>
<strong>Used those junction points to isolate only the relevant portions of the longer trail lines.</strong><br>
The Red Trail could continue beyond the loop while the same physical corridor could also help define a smaller public route.
</div>
</div>

<div class="step">
<div class="step-num">4</div>
<div>
<strong>Combined those portions into a new conceptual public route.</strong><br>
We called it <strong>Proposed Loop A</strong> only so we could see what the end-user experience might look like.
</div>
</div>

---

## Why the junction points mattered

The existing features did not meet in a perfectly clean, purpose-built loop.

The short line connected into the **middle of longer Red Trail features**, and the geometry was offset by a few feet in places.

<div class="two-col">

<div class="card">
<span class="badge badge-current">Existing data</span>

### Physical trail pieces

The data told us where the trail lines were collected, but not necessarily where a visitor-facing route should begin or end.

</div>

<div class="card">
<span class="badge badge-proposed">GIS pilot</span>

### Junction points

We used the connection locations as logical break points, then extracted only the portions needed for the conceptual loop.

</div>

</div>

<div class="footer-note">This is a good example of why future collection should explicitly capture junctions/intersections rather than asking GIS to infer them later.</div>

---

## Existing structure vs. proposed public concept

<div class="two-col">

<div class="card">

### Existing structure

<span class="badge badge-current">Internal network</span>

- Red Trail
- Red Trail
- Red Trail
- Longer route continues beyond the local area
- Segment boundaries reflect how the data was collected

<div class="route-line gray"></div>

<strong>Useful for:</strong> maintaining a physical network and retaining legacy information.

</div>

<div class="card">

### Proposed public concept

<span class="badge badge-proposed">Visitor-facing route</span>

- **Proposed Loop A**
- Shorter, understandable loop
- Built from portions of the existing physical network
- Existing Red Trail can still continue beyond it

<div class="route-line green"></div>

<strong>Useful for:</strong> public navigation, maps, trail descriptions, mileage, and route-level communication.

</div>

</div>

---

## What this does — and does not — prove

<div class="three-col">

<div class="card">

### It does show

The current geometry can sometimes be reorganized into clearer visitor-facing routes.

</div>

<div class="card">

### It does not show

That GIS can reliably reconstruct every trail in the park without field verification or Parks input.

</div>

<div class="card">

### Most importantly

It gives us a concrete example to discuss before committing to a larger recollection effort.

</div>

</div>

---

## Why we cannot automate this for every trail

This worked because a person could look at a small area and make a reasonable interpretation of the physical network.

Across the full park, GIS still cannot confidently infer:

- which intersections are intentional;
- where one public route should stop and another should begin;
- whether a connector is a visitor route, maintenance access, shared corridor, or something else;
- which long routes should remain long and which areas are better represented as loops or shorter routes;
- which names are official, historical, temporary, or simply artifacts of the current database.

<div class="callout">

A script can help identify geometry and connection points. **It cannot make Parks-management or visitor-experience decisions for us.**

</div>

---

## Proposed field-collection approach

<div class="three-col">

<div class="card">

### 1. Use the current data

Bring the existing trail network into Field Maps as a read-only reference.

</div>

<div class="card">

### 2. Verify with Trimble

Walk representative areas and collect/verify:

- centerlines
- junctions
- intersections
- true endpoints
- shared corridors
- questionable gaps

</div>

<div class="card">

### 3. Update selectively

Classify existing data as:

- keep
- repair
- verify
- recollect

We do not need to automatically assume every mile must be recollected.

</div>

</div>

---

## How we think future trail data could work

<div class="two-col">

<div class="card">

### Internal Parks / GIS network

<span class="badge badge-current">Detailed</span>

Physical trail segments with stable IDs.

Possible fields:

- Segment ID
- surface
- condition
- accessibility
- status
- maintenance notes
- field verification date
- shared-corridor / connector role

These pieces can remain detailed because Parks may need them operationally.

</div>

<div class="card">

### Public trail routes

<span class="badge badge-proposed">Simple</span>

Routes assembled from the underlying physical segments.

Possible fields:

- public trail name
- route type (loop / out-and-back / connector)
- mileage
- difficulty
- surface
- blaze/color
- public status
- visitor description

The public does not need to see segment IDs or internal connector names.

</div>

</div>

---

## Naming needs Parks

<div class="callout callout-green">

GIS can identify geometry and propose a structure. **Parks should have the authority to decide official trail names and route identities.**

</div>

For the pilot, names like **Proposed Loop A** are intentionally generic.

What we would want from Parks is help answering questions such as:

- Does this smaller loop represent how visitors actually use the area?
- Should it have its own name?
- Should the larger Red Trail remain one public route, or should portions of it be presented differently?
- Are there locally used names that are not represented in the GIS?
- Which connectors should be visible to visitors, and which should remain internal?

---

## Why loops are worth discussing

A long named trail can make sense from an internal management perspective while still being difficult for a visitor to interpret.

A visitor may be looking for:

- a 0.5-mile walk;
- a 1-mile loop;
- a route back to the same parking area;
- a family-friendly option;
- an easy way to understand where a trail starts and ends.

<div class="big-question">

The physical network does not have to change for the public route structure to become easier to understand.

</div>

---

## What we are proposing to Parks

<div class="callout">

<strong>Use this case study as a starting point.</strong>

We would like to work with Parks to test a better collection and route-organization method in a small area before deciding what should happen across the entire trail system.

</div>

A practical next step could be:

1. Pick one representative area of Mercer County Park.
2. Walk it with Parks using the Trimble / Field Maps.
3. Compare what exists on the ground with the current GIS.
4. Agree on how junctions, connectors, shared corridors, and route names should be handled.
5. Use that pilot to establish a repeatable collection standard for the rest of the park.

---

## The point of the pilot

<div class="big-question">

We are not saying, “the old data is bad.”

We are saying, “we are asking the data to do something new.”

</div>

The existing data gave us a strong starting point.

The next step is figuring out, together, how to structure it so that it supports both **how Parks manages the trail system** and **how the public experiences it**.

---

## Discussion

<div class="two-col">

<div class="card">

### Questions for Parks

- How do you currently think about individual routes?
- Which trail names are official?
- Are there existing loops or commonly used route names not captured in GIS?
- What information would be most useful for maintenance and field staff?

</div>

<div class="card">

### Questions for GIS

- Which geometry can be retained?
- Where do we need Trimble verification?
- How should internal segments relate to public routes?
- What should the future Field Maps workflow capture?

</div>

</div>
